title: Magnetic Particle Weld Inspection | MPI of Welds, US
description: On-site magnetic particle weld inspection (MT of welds) to ASME, AWS D1.1 and API 1104 criteria, mobilized across the US. Request a quote with your weld list.
h1: Magnetic Particle Weld Inspection: MT of Welds Across the United States
html:
Magnetic particle weld inspection (MPI of welds, MT weld inspection) finds cracks and other surface-breaking and shallow subsurface discontinuities in ferromagnetic weld metal and heat-affected zone. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians across the United States to fabrication shops, pipelines, plants, yards and job sites to examine welds to ASME, AWS or API acceptance criteria and to deliver a report your inspector can accept or reject against the code. You can request a magnetic particle weld inspection quote with the weld list and code.

What magnetic particle testing of welds finds

MT is the method most inspectors reach for when the question is "is there a crack at this weld?" in carbon and low-alloy steel. A magnetized weld leaks flux where a discontinuity interrupts the field, and fine iron particles gather at that leakage and form a visible line. The indication is sharp, quick to read and shows the length of the flaw immediately. Typical findings on welds are:

  • Toe cracks and heat-affected-zone cracks, including hydrogen-assisted cold cracking in thick or high-strength sections.
  • Longitudinal and transverse weld metal cracks, crater cracks at stop-starts and arc strikes that have hardened.
  • Lack of fusion at the sidewall when it breaks the surface or lies just beneath a thin cap.
  • Slag lines and porosity that open to the surface, and linear indications at grinding gouges and temporary attachment scars.
  • Root-side and back-gouged surfaces that were ground clean and need a check before the next pass or fill.

MT does not size depth, and it does not replace visual examination: undercut, overlap, reinforcement and profile are visual calls, and the weld surface must be visually acceptable before magnetic particle work starts. It is also limited to ferromagnetic material. Austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys are not magnetic, so those welds go to liquid penetrant instead. See our liquid penetrant testing service for that work.

Codes and standards that drive MT of welds

The method follows the code that governs the weld, not a house preference. The procedure we write or follow is built from the technique requirements in ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709, then the acceptance criteria come from the construction or service code:

  • ASME B31.3 process piping: examination requirements and acceptance criteria for welds are in the code's examination chapter, with the owner setting the extent of examination.
  • AWS D1.1 structural welding: Clause 8 covers inspection, with acceptance criteria for statically loaded structures that differ from cyclically loaded ones.
  • API 1104 cross-country pipelines: MT is used on weld areas, and the standard sets its own acceptance limits for cracks and other imperfections.
  • ASME Section VIII and Section I vessel and boiler fabrication call on Section V techniques with acceptance in the construction code or its appendices.

Who decides acceptance matters. Atlantis applies the code criteria the owner or the fabricator's quality plan names and reports every indication with its size and location. The owner's inspector, the engineer of record or the authorized inspector makes the accept, repair or reject decision on the weld. Where an owner needs a written procedure or a demonstration to the code, see NDT technical procedure development and procedure qualification and demonstration.

Yokes, prods and field direction

Most weld work in the field uses a handheld electromagnetic yoke, which magnetizes the weld between its legs with the pole spacing adjusted to the joint. Yokes are quick to set up, produce no arc burns and can be used on pipe, plate and structural shapes. Competent technique rests on a few details:

  • Yoke lifting power. Before use, the yoke is checked against the test weight the procedure specifies at the maximum pole spacing planned. An AC yoke and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke have different required lifting power, and a yoke that fails the check is not used.
  • Two perpendicular magnetizations. A crack is found best when the field crosses it at close to a right angle. Each weld area is therefore magnetized in two directions roughly perpendicular to each other, so transverse and longitudinal cracks both show.
  • Overlap and coverage. Each yoke position overlaps the last, and the effective area is limited to the zone the procedure allows around the poles. The weld and the adjacent base metal specified in the code are covered, not just the cap.
  • Prods. Prod contacts pass current through the part and can leave arc burns and local hardening. Many specifications restrict or forbid prods on pressure-retaining and high-strength material, so we use them only where the procedure and owner permit and the spot is dressed afterward.

Surface condition limits sensitivity. Heavy spatter, scale, paint and rough weld ripple can hold particles and give false indications, so the procedure states the cleaning required before magnetization. A weld that must be examined as welded has a different procedure from one that has been ground flush.

Wet fluorescent versus visible dry powder

Two particle choices cover most field weld work. Visible dry powder is applied as a light cloud over a magnetized surface and works well on rough, hot or outdoor welds; the color is chosen for contrast with the weld surface. Wet suspension, either visible or fluorescent, flows over the surface and gives the highest sensitivity to fine tight cracks. Fluorescent particles are viewed under ultraviolet light, so the technician needs a darkened work area and the ultraviolet intensity at the surface, and the ambient white light level, are measured and recorded against the procedure limits. Visible methods require adequate white light at the surface instead.

For a root pass checked after back gouging or a thick-wall weld subject to cracking, wet fluorescent is usually the more sensitive tool. For a long field weld in daylight or a high-temperature surface, visible dry powder may be the practical choice. The code and the owner's procedure fix the allowed combinations; we point out where a different technique would improve the odds of finding a crack and let the owner decide.

When in the weld sequence MT is performed

Timing changes what the examination can find and what a repair costs. Common hold points include:

  1. Root and back-gouged surfaces before the next pass buries them.
  2. Hot pass or intermediate layers on heavy sections or crack-prone alloys, so a defect is ground out before more metal is added.
  3. Final cap and toes after the weld is visually accepted, before painting, coating or insulation.
  4. After post-weld heat treatment or hydrotest where the code or owner wants a check for cracks that appear late. Delayed cracking in some steels is the reason a code may wait to examine.
  5. After repair grinding and rewelding to confirm the excavation was clean and the repair weld is sound.

When a project defines the examination point, we work to that point. When it does not, we ask the owner's quality lead or inspector rather than assuming one.

Demagnetization and cleaning afterward

A part can keep residual magnetism after testing. That matters when it will be welded again, since a residual field deflects the arc, when it is a bearing surface, and when it moves into a machining operation where chips cling. Procedures state whether demagnetization is required and how much residual field is acceptable. We demagnetize when the procedure calls for it, remove the particles and suspension, and leave the weld clean so coating or further fabrication is not affected. Where particle residue could contaminate a service environment, we say so in the report so the owner can clean further.

What the report contains

A weld MT report should let a different inspector reconstruct what was done. Ours lists:

  • Component or weld identification, joint type and material, with a sketch or weld map reference.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the governing code and edition.
  • Equipment: yoke model, lifting-power check, particle type and lot, light meter and ultraviolet meter with calibration status.
  • Surface condition and cleaning, temperature of the part when it was examined, and the examination dates.
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, and the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Every indication, with location, orientation and length, and whether it is accepted or rejected against the named criteria, with a photograph or marked sketch.
  • Any repair examinations and the final status of each weld.

The report records conditions and results. The accept or reject decision on a weld belongs to the owner or the party named in the contract.

What to send for a quote

  • Weld list, drawings or weld maps with joint IDs and quantities.
  • Material grades and thicknesses, including any stainless or alloy welds that need penetrant instead.
  • Governing code, edition and acceptance criteria, and the owner's written procedure if one exists.
  • Required particle type, and whether the work is shop, field or in-service.
  • Surface condition, coating, insulation removal and who provides access, scaffolding or lifts.
  • Temperature at the weld, site address, safety orientation, badging and permit requirements.

Planning realities for weld MT in the United States

Fabrication shops are usually the simplest sites: stable lighting, grounded power and clean surfaces. Field welds on pipelines, tanks and structures bring weather, wind that blows powder away, night work and tight spaces, and fluorescent work needs a dark enclosure or tent. Hot surfaces change which particle can be used, so tell us the metal temperature. Refinery and plant work adds hot-work and confined-space permits and site safety training, and offshore and marine yards add transport and access limits. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and Atlantis has no office near the site, so access, permits and lodging are part of the plan we build with you.

Where we work in the United States

  • Houston: refinery, petrochemical and pipe fabrication welds along the Ship Channel.
  • Tulsa: pipeline and pressure-vessel fabrication and repair welds across the Mid-Continent.
  • Pittsburgh: structural and heavy steel fabrication and mill-related repairs.
  • Chicago: structural steel, rail and heavy equipment welds.
  • Birmingham: pipe, foundry and fabricated steel welds in the Southeast.
  • Peoria: earthmoving and heavy machinery weldments.
  • Cleveland: steel processing and manufacturing weld inspection.
  • Beaumont: refinery and shipyard welds on the Gulf Coast.

Related work by industry is in fabrication, pipeline, offshore and oilfield inspection, and the full weld inspection service explains how MT fits with visual and ultrasonic examination.

Training your own MT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis provides MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training based on SNT-TC-1A, plus the magnetic particle simulator for practice. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own personnel under its written practice, and our written practice development service helps you set that up.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and it does not make weld repair or fitness-for-service decisions. Specialist techniques beyond MT, PT and UT are outside this page. We report indications against the criteria you give us, and your engineer, inspector or authorized inspector decides what happens to the weld.

faq.q: What is the difference between MT and PT on welds?
faq.a: MT uses the leakage field around a flaw and works only on ferromagnetic steel, finding surface and shallow subsurface cracks quickly. PT uses a penetrant that enters surface-breaking flaws and works on any non-porous material, including stainless steel and aluminum, but only finds flaws open to the surface.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless steel welds?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel or nickel alloys, because they are not magnetic enough to hold a useful field. Ferritic and martensitic stainless grades can be examined by MT. For austenitic welds, liquid penetrant is the normal surface method.

faq.q: Why are welds magnetized in two directions?
faq.a: Flux leakage is strongest when the field crosses a flaw at a right angle. A crack parallel to the field gives little or no indication, so Article 7 and ASTM E709 call for two directions roughly perpendicular to each other so cracks in any orientation are caught.

faq.q: Are prods allowed for weld MT?
faq.a: Sometimes. Prods can leave arc burns and local hard spots, and many owner specifications restrict or ban them on pressure-retaining or high-strength steel. We use prods only when the procedure and the owner permit them and dress any burns afterward.

faq.q: Do you need a dark space for fluorescent MT?
faq.a: Yes. Fluorescent particles are examined under ultraviolet light in a darkened area, and the ultraviolet intensity at the surface and the ambient white light are measured against the procedure. Outdoors we use a tent or enclosure, or choose visible particles if the code allows.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects weld indications?
faq.a: The owner, the engineer of record or the party named in the contract applies the code acceptance criteria and decides. We record each indication with its location and size and report it against the criteria you supply, so the decision maker has the facts.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote MT of welds?
faq.a: A weld list or drawings, material and thickness, governing code and edition, any written procedure, surface and temperature conditions, access arrangements, and the site address with safety and badging requirements. With those, we can scope the crew and the report.

faq.q: Can MT find subsurface lack of fusion?
faq.a: Only if the flaw is near enough to the surface to disturb the field, and then the indication is weak. Buried lack of fusion and inclusions are usually found with ultrasonic testing, so many weld programs pair MT with UT.

faq.q: Does MT need to be done before or after coating?
faq.a: Before. Paint and thick coatings reduce sensitivity, and the code or procedure states the maximum coating thickness allowed. Welds are examined bare or with a controlled thin coating, then coated after acceptance.

faq.q: Do you inspect pipeline girth welds with MT?
faq.a: We perform MT on weld areas where the owner's procedure and the applicable standard, such as API 1104, call for it. The owner decides acceptance, and we do not run in-line inspection tools.
